patient_information: A 28-year-old Malawian man, a fisherman from a town on the southern shore of Lake Malawi, was diagnosed with arterial hypertension 2 years prior but never took prescribed antihypertensive drugs; his recent HIV test was negative.
chief_complaint: Progressive shortness of breath over the past 5 days.
history_of_present_illness: He reports orthopnoea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea, bilateral flank pain (continuous and dull), and constant nausea, without cough or fever.
exposure_and_epidemiology: Being a fisherman, the patient has been in regular contact with Schistosoma haematobium-infested water in Lake Malawi.
vitals: Blood pressure 200/130 mmHg, pulse 66 bpm, temperature 36.8°C, and respiratory rate 32 breath cycles per minute.
physical_exam: The patient is in respiratory distress, has notably pale conjunctivae, a slightly displaced apex beat with clear and regular heart sounds, no raised jugular venous pressure, bilateral fine crackles over the lung bases, a flat and non-tender abdomen, bilateral renal angle tenderness, ballottable kidneys, and no peripheral oedema.
labs_and_diagnostics: WBC 3.8 x10^9/L, Haemoglobin 6.0 mg/dL, MCV 92 fL, Platelets 187 x10^9/L, Creatinine 1200 µmol/L, BUN 89.3 mmol/L, K+ 7.2 mmol/l. Chest radiograph on admission (Figure 7.1) shows pulmonary congestion. Ultrasound showed bilateral hydronephrosis with massive dilatation of the renal pelvis and calyces and very thin remaining renal parenchyma. Cystoscopy revealed a hyperaemic mucosa with multiple 'sandy patches'.
differential_diagnosis: Combined left-sided cardiac failure and renal failure, with chronic schistosomiasis with hydronephrosis being one of the top differential diagnoses.
management_and_clinical_course: Despite high doses of furosemide, the patient remained oliguric. Glucose and insulin were administered for hyperkalaemia. A bilateral percutaneous nephrostomy was done, and peritoneal dialysis was started in the intensive care unit. The patient improved rapidly, with cessation of vomiting and drowsiness and disappearance of friction rub, and was discharged home on PD. Two months later, he was readmitted with fever and abdominal pain, treated for suspected bacterial peritonitis, but died 3 weeks later.
final_diagnosis: Urogenital schistosomiasis with combined left-sided cardiac failure and end-stage renal disease.

images.caption: Cystoscopy findings of a patient with urogenital schistosomiasis. The white arrows show 'sandy patches' (left) and hyperaemia of the bladder mucosa (top).
